blog.title: Behind the interface.
blog.intro: Short, practical notes on frontend development, design and the user experience.

interfaces.title: Good interfaces start with small details
interfaces.excerpt: Spacing, hierarchy and states: the decisions that make a simple interface feel effortless.
interfaces.body1: When someone lands on a page, its main purpose should be clear. One primary heading, readable copy and an obvious action are a useful starting point. Choose size and spacing according to the importance of the content; giving everything equal emphasis splits attention.
interfaces.heading2: Design more than the ideal state
interfaces.body2: A form error, an empty list, loading data and a long heading are all part of the design. A disabled button and a helpful field error tell people what is happening. Considering these states early reduces improvised fixes later.
interfaces.body3: Making a screen narrower means more than stacking columns. Test with long text, keyboard navigation and different languages. Links should be easy to select, headings should stay inside their containers, and essential information should never depend on hovering.

motion.title: Movement should serve the design
motion.excerpt: Animation can guide attention. The question is what it explains, rather than how much moves.
motion.body1: When an element changes state, animation can help explain the relationship. Keeping a laptop in place while changing only its screen is a simple example. A stable frame lets the viewer focus on new content instead of chasing a moving object.
motion.heading2: Keep scrolling in the user's control
motion.body2: A scroll-driven scene connects motion to progress through a page. Define the beginning, the end and the interval for reading ahead of time. On mobile, sequential sections can provide a more comfortable experience than an extended pinned sequence.
motion.heading3: The motion-free version must still work
motion.body3: Some people prefer less movement. Respect prefers-reduced-motion and keep important content independent of animation. When motion is disabled, navigation, text and controls must remain accessible and usable.

localization.title: Three languages, one comfortable experience
localization.excerpt: Translation is more than replacing words: layout and user journeys need to adapt too.
localization.body1: Keeping translations in separate files makes it easier to compare the same content across languages. Include button labels, form errors and screen reader descriptions alongside headings. Even a small label left in another language can interrupt the experience.
localization.heading2: Keep the current page when switching
localization.body2: Someone reading the CV should still see the CV after choosing another language. Switching languages should not send them back to the homepage every time. A language prefix in the URL makes shared links clearer and navigation more predictable.
localization.heading3: Try the layout with longer text
localization.body3: The same idea occupies different amounts of space in different languages. Fixed-width buttons and single-line heading containers can overflow. Open each language at mobile and desktop sizes to check readability and line breaks.

portfolio.title: How I created my portfolio
portfolio.excerpt: From a visual idea to an animated Next.js website: my references, the video generation prompt and the complete frontend brief.
portfolio.referenceAlt: Original portfolio design: Arzu, a developer ID card and a MacBook on a blue background
portfolio.referenceCaption: The starting point — the original visual reference for my portfolio.
portfolio.heading1: I started with the visual identity.
portfolio.body1: My visual identity is at the center of this portfolio: a blue gradient, oversized name typography, my portrait with a MacBook, a hanging developer card and colorful folders. I prepared separate references for the opening screen and the project showcase. The portrait, card, laptop and decorations were kept as individual PNG assets so they could be animated independently on the website.
portfolio.heading2: From a still design to a motion direction.
portfolio.body2: I divided the video brief into three scenes: a quiet introduction, a move toward the laptop and a screen reveal. The prompt explicitly asks to preserve my face, outfit, card and text. The video below is the reference I supplied for the website animation; the complete prompt describes that intended direction.
portfolio.videoCaption: Animation reference · about 10 seconds. The prompt requests 4K/60 FPS as a target; the supplied file is 1280 × 720 at 24 FPS.
portfolio.scene1Text: Gentle typing, a softly swinging ID card and subtle depth in the floating folders.
portfolio.scene2Text: The camera approaches the MacBook and the composition transitions without a hard cut.
portfolio.scene3Text: The black screen powers on and project previews appear in sequence.
portfolio.heading3: Then I turned the idea into a website.
portfolio.body3: For the frontend brief I chose Next.js App Router, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, GSAP and next-intl. I asked for a scroll-controlled pinned scene, project transitions inside a stationary MacBook, separate pages and three languages. The static portrait on the website cannot move its hands independently; transforms and crossfades approximate the camera transition. The second scene uses white, as explicitly requested in the written brief.

portfolio.takeawayLabel: What I learned from the process
portfolio.takeawayTitle: A useful prompt starts with a specific reference.
portfolio.takeawayText: Be clear about what must stay unchanged, what moves and how the result should be checked. Reference images, scene timing and technical requirements establish the direction; responsiveness, accessibility and working navigation still need to be verified in the actual website.

projectsPage.title: Things I've built.
projectsPage.intro: From commercial platforms to personal and open-source projects — in each one I turned a design into a working product.

items.readly: A full-stack book review platform: users register, log in, explore books, write reviews and track their reading statistics. Books can be filtered and sorted, average ratings viewed, and users level up based on how many books they've read. Includes JWT authentication, a profile system with level and avatar, and admin content management.
items.aionTimer: A time-management web app built with TypeScript: custom countdowns for productivity, study or rest sessions, visual and audio alerts, and immersive 3D visuals with Three.js. Built with Next.js, Tailwind CSS, Redux, Zod, JWT and MongoDB.
items.toast: A lightweight toast notification library written in TypeScript, with distinctive animations, positioning options and interactive behaviors. The toast component is fully functional and easy to add to any React/Next.js project; the modal feature is still in development.
items.hubfolio: A portfolio website built with HTML, CSS and Vanilla JS, with engaging scroll-based animations and a clean, responsive design.
items.aionAnalyze: A PDF analysis tool: upload PDF files to read their content and get a concise answer. The frontend is built with Next.js, the backend with Node.js and FastAPI.
items.voice: A Next.js app with elements controlled by speech: scroll to the top, rotate a button, make a button jump and kick a ball across the screen. Uses the Web Speech API through Annyang.
items.metraj: A website for buying and selling apartments. I built the frontend; the backend uses Fastify.
items.glabbe: A full-stack appointment management platform for professionals.
items.loyalty: A loyalty system: a React-based PWA plus a React Native mobile app.
items.boulvard: A clinic management system with a responsive interface.
items.foodlens: An AI-powered risk analysis app for food safety.
items.evisa: An online electronic visa application platform for travelers.
items.clomni: I was part of the team behind the Clomni website rebranding.
items.alfinx: Front-end internship at AlfinX, a company building AI-based solutions for business automation.

about.bioTitle: From design to working product — 3+ years of real experience.

about.bio2: I turn Figma designs into pixel-perfect code with a strong focus on performance, accessibility, SEO and multilingual support. My backend experience with Node.js, Express, MongoDB and Supabase helps me work smoothly with backend teams and build clean API integrations.
about.bio3: Beyond code, I design UI/UX in Figma and create video and visual content with AI tools. My goal is to build digital products that look great and deliver real business results.
